clinicalPearls: Caused by de novo truncating variants in ASXL3, a polycomb group chromatin regulator related to ASXL1 that participates in histone deubiquitination and polycomb-mediated gene silencing
Presents with severe global developmental delay, absent or very limited speech and prominent muscular hypotonia
Feeding difficulties and poor postnatal growth are common in infancy
The facial appearance includes arched eyebrows, a prominent forehead, hypertelorism, a prominent nasal bridge and anteverted nares
Autistic features and behavioural difficulties are frequently observed
Although mechanistically related to Bohring-Opitz syndrome, it lacks the characteristic BOS posture and is not associated with the same Wilms tumour risk
Diagnosis is molecular, identifying a de novo loss-of-function ASXL3 variant, with an emerging methylation episignature aiding interpretation
reference.pathophysiology: ASXL3 encodes a member of the additional sex combs-like family of polycomb group proteins, which regulate chromatin by influencing histone ubiquitination and the balance of polycomb-mediated gene repression. Constitutional truncating variants disturb this epigenetic regulation, deranging the developmental programmes of gene expression that guide neuronal maturation and craniofacial patterning. The resulting dysregulation produces severe intellectual disability, speech impairment, hypotonia and a distinctive facial gestalt; although ASXL3 is closely related to ASXL1, differences in their developmental roles explain why Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome lacks the fixed posture and tumour predisposition seen in Bohring-Opitz syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Other severe syndromic intellectual disability with absent speech
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing to detect de novo truncating ASXL3 variants
DNA methylation episignature analysis where available
Neurodevelopmental and behavioural assessment including autism evaluation
Assessment of feeding and swallowing in infancy
Brain MRI if structural anomalies or seizures are suspected
Growth monitoring for failure to thrive
redFlags: Severe feeding difficulty with faltering growth in infancy
Recurrent aspiration linked to hypotonia and swallowing problems
Developmental regression, which would prompt reassessment
reference.prognosis: The disorder causes lifelong severe intellectual disability with major speech limitation and dependence on augmentative communication; survival is generally not curtailed in the absence of severe feeding or respiratory complications, and management focuses on developmental, feeding and behavioural support.
pitfalls: Confusing Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome with Bohring-Opitz syndrome and wrongly instituting Wilms tumour surveillance or expecting the BOS posture
Misdiagnosing the child as Angelman or Pitt-Hopkins syndrome without appropriate molecular testing
Delaying augmentative communication while awaiting speech that may not develop
Underestimating early feeding difficulties driven by hypotonia
references: Nature Reviews — polycomb chromatin regulators in development and disease
management: No disease-specific treatment exists, so care is supportive and multidisciplinary through neurodevelopmental and genetics services
Early intervention with physiotherapy and occupational therapy for hypotonia, and augmentative and alternative communication given absent or very limited speech
Speech and language therapy with structured educational and behavioural support including autism-focused strategies
Assess feeding and swallowing in infancy with dietetic support and enteral feeding if growth falters
Monitor growth and development, and investigate and treat seizures if they arise
Provide genetic counselling, noting that the ASXL3 variants are typically de novo with low recurrence risk, while discussing the possibility of germline mosaicism
